segments.english: The sages taught in the language of the Mishnah; blessed is He who chose them and their teaching. Rabbi Meir says: Whoever engages in Torah for its own sake merits many things. Not only that, but the entire world is worthwhile for his sake. He is called friend, beloved, one who loves the Omnipresent, one who loves creatures, one who gladdens the Omnipresent, one who gladdens creatures. It clothes him in humility and awe, it fits him to be righteous, devout, upright and faithful, it keeps him far from sin and draws him near to merit. People derive from him the benefit of counsel and sound wisdom, understanding and strength, as it is said (Proverbs 8): "Mine are counsel and sound wisdom; I am understanding; mine is strength." It gives him kingship and dominion and the probing of judgment; the secrets of Torah are revealed to him; he becomes like a spring that grows ever stronger and like a river that never ceases; he is modest and patient, and he forgives insult done to him; it makes him great and raises him above all the works.

grammar: This opening sentence is the standard introduction to the "baraita of the Sages of the Mishnah" (the Kinyan Torah): the phrase בִּלְשׁוֹן הַמִּשְׁנָה marks what follows as Mishnaic (Tannaitic) teaching, and בָּרוּךְ שֶׁבָּחַר is a short doxology.
The long run of participles in the third clause (אוֹהֵב, מְשַׂמֵּחַ ...) is a list of descriptive titles after נִקְרָא; מְשַׂמֵּחַ is a Piel participle, "one who causes gladness".

From וּמַלְבַּשְׁתּוֹ to וּמְרוֹמַמְתּוֹ the feminine singular participles (מַלְבֶּשֶׁת, מַכְשֶׁרֶת, מְרַחֶקֶת, מְקָרֶבֶת, נוֹתֶנֶת ...) have the feminine noun תוֹרָה as their unstated subject, with the masculine suffix -ו referring to the one who engages in Torah.
נֶהֱנִין and מְגַלִּין are masculine plural participles with no expressed subject, i.e. impersonal ("people benefit", "they reveal" = "are revealed").
Mishnaic Hebrew uses שֶׁ- for "that", "who", "for"; so שֶׁכָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ ... is "that the whole world ..." after אֶלָּא "but".
segments.note: כְדַי הוּא לוֹ means roughly "it is enough, it is worth it, for him": the whole world is (worth the) trouble or existence for his sake; the Hebrew does not say who benefits. The subject of the feminine participles is the Torah (see grammar). וֶהֱוֵי is an imperative ("be!") standing in a run of third-person descriptions; the English follows the sense ("he is modest and patient") and the imperative is recorded in the apparatus. הַמַּעֲשִׂים, "the works", can mean God's creations or deeds; the English keeps the literal "works".
apparatus: Proverbs 8:14 is quoted (לִי עֵצָה וְתוּשִׁיָּה אֲנִי בִינָה לִי גְבוּרָה), translated here from the Hebrew of the mishnah.
Alternative for 6:1.90: "And be modest and patient" read as a direct address (imperative), as the form וֶהֱוֵי literally is.
Vilna variants: 6:1.2 החכמים (with article), 6:1.29 ריע for רֵעַ, 6:1.59 ממנה for מִמֶּנּוּ; Vilna lacks the verse citation labels (משלי ח).

segments.english: Rabbi Joshua son of Levi said: Every single day a heavenly voice goes out from Mount Horeb, proclaiming and saying: Woe to the creatures for the insult done to the Torah! For whoever does not engage in Torah is called rebuked, as it is said (Proverbs 11): "A gold ring in a pig's snout: a beautiful woman who has turned from discretion." And it says (Exodus 32): "The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets." Do not read ḥarut (engraved) but ḥerut (freedom), for you have no free person except one who engages in the study of Torah. And whoever engages in the study of Torah, such a person is exalted, as it is said (Numbers 21): "And from Mattanah to Nahaliel, and from Nahaliel to Bamoth."

grammar: בַּת קוֹל, literally "daughter of a voice", is a technical term for a heavenly voice that makes God's will known after prophecy has ceased; it is in the construct state, and יוֹצֵאת, מַכְרֶזֶת and אוֹמֶרֶת are feminine participles agreeing with it.
וָיוֹם repeats יוֹם with a conjunction for emphasis: "day and day", i.e. every single day.

מֵעֶלְבּוֹנָהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה uses the Mishnaic genitive particle שֶׁל; the feminine suffix -הּ anticipates תּוֹרָה (a "split construct"): "from her insult, of Torah". The insult is the one Torah suffers, when people neglect her.

The citation אֵין לְךָ ... אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁ- is the Mishnaic idiom "you have no X except one who ..."; אַל תִּקְרָא ... אֶלָּא is a formula of reading-variation (a midrashic re-vocalization), here exploiting the two readings חָרוּת / חֵרוּת of the same consonants חרות.

Numbers 21:19 is a list of stopping-places; the mishnah relies on the meanings of the names, mattanah "gift", naḥaliel "inheritance (or portion) of God", bamot "heights", to describe a rise by stages. The English translates the verse as place names, as the Hebrew has them.
segments.note: Vilna's text differs at 6:2.71-72 (בתורה תדיר, "constantly in Torah"). נָזוּף is the passive participle of נזף, "rebuked, censured". סָרַת טָעַם: טַעַם is "taste, discernment, good sense"; the verse says the woman has turned aside from it. The English for בַּת קוֹל gives the meaning "heavenly voice" and the literal sense is in the phrase literal. הֲרֵי זֶה (lit. "behold this one") is rendered "such a person".
apparatus: Proverbs 11:22; Exodus 32:16; Numbers 21:19; all quoted from the Hebrew of the mishnah.
Vilna variants: 6:2.43 and 6:2.53 spell הלוחות (full spelling); 6:2.58 spells חירות; 6:2.71-72 reads בתורה תדיר for בְּתַלְמוּד תּוֹרָה.

segments.english: One who learns from his fellow a single chapter, or a single halakhah, or a single verse, or a single saying, or even a single letter, must treat him with honor. For so we find with David, king of Israel, who learned from Ahithophel only two things, yet called him his teacher, his companion and his familiar, as it is said (Psalms 55): "And you, a man of my own rank, my companion and my familiar." Is this not an argument from the lesser to the greater? If David, king of Israel, who learned from Ahithophel only two things, called him his teacher, his companion and his familiar, then one who learns from his fellow a single chapter, or a single halakhah, or a single verse, or a single saying, or even a single letter, how much more so must he treat him with honor. And there is no honor but Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 3): "The wise shall inherit honor," and (Proverbs 28): "and the blameless shall inherit good"; and there is no good but Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 4): "For I have given you good teaching; do not forsake my Torah."

grammar: הַלּוֹמֵד is a participle with the article used as a noun, "the one who learns", the subject of the whole sentence; צָרִיךְ לִנְהוֹג בּוֹ כָבוֹד is "must conduct honor toward him" (נָהַג + בְּ-).
שֶׁכֵּן מָצִינוּ ("for so we found") is a formula introducing a proof from precedent; שֶׁלֹּא ... אֶלָּא means "who ... only".

וַהֲלֹא דְבָרִים קַל וָחֹמֶר is the formula of the a fortiori argument, "light and heavy": what holds in the lighter case (two things learned) holds all the more in the weightier (a chapter, a law ...); the second half is closed by עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה, "how much more so".
אֵין ... אֶלָּא ("there is no X but Y") is a definitional formula: "honor" in the verse means Torah, "good" in the verse means Torah, which links the three verses.

The citations are all verses with direct speech: Psalms 55:14 is addressed to a friend (2nd person), Proverbs 3:35 and 28:10 are third-person statements, and Proverbs 4:2 is God's address (1st person) to the people.
segments.note: אַלּוּף is "tame; friend, intimate; chief"; the English "companion" follows the sense of Psalm 55 and the sequence rabbo-alufo-meyudda'o (teacher, companion, familiar), but "chief, guide" is possible (see lexicon sense 3). כְּעֶרְכִּי is "according to my rank/estimate", i.e. "my equal". The English "halakhah" keeps the technical term for a received rule of law. בִּלְבַד "only". תּוֹרָתִי in the quoted verse is "my teaching", a gloss of "my Torah"; the English keeps "Torah" as the decisions require.
apparatus: Psalms 55:14; Proverbs 3:35; Proverbs 28:10; Proverbs 4:2; all quoted from the Hebrew of the mishnah.

Vilna variants: 6:3.2 and 6:3.66 מחבירו; 6:3.15 and 6:3.79 אפילו; 6:3.29 and 6:3.56 מאחיתופל; 6:3.34 וקראו; 6:3.37, 6:3.45, 6:3.64 with ו in מיודע-; 6:3.49 וחומר; 6:3.119 תעזובו; Vilna lacks the third "או" at 6:3.14 and 6:3.78 (reading "or a single saying, even a single letter").

If you do this, (Psalms 128) "Happy are you, and it shall be well with you": happy are you in this world, and it shall be well with you in the world to come.

grammar: כַּךְ הִיא דַּרְכָּהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה: the feminine suffix -הּ again anticipates תּוֹרָה (שֶׁל construction); כַּךְ is "so, thus", and the sentence reads "so is the way of Torah".

The imperfects תֹּאכַל, תִשְׁתֶּה, תִּישַׁן, תִּחְיֶה are 2nd masculine singular with a force between a command and a description ("you shall"); חַיֵּי צַעַר תִּחְיֶה is a cognate accusative, "live a life of hardship".
בִּמְשׂוּרָה is "by measure": a small measured quantity; the phrase pairs with בְּמֶלַח to describe a bare diet.
The verse Psalms 128:2 has אַשְׁרֶיךָ וְטוֹב לָךְ; the mishnah then splits the pair between this world and the world to come, repeating אַשְׁרֶיךָ.
segments.note: וּבַתּוֹרָה אַתָּה עָמֵל puts the object of effort first for emphasis ("and in Torah you toil"); the explicit pronoun אַתָּה with a participle is the Mishnaic present. The verse is read as describing the reward, "happy are you" (אַשְׁרֶיךָ) being the Hebrew exclamation of blessedness.
apparatus: Psalms 128:2, quoted from the Hebrew of the mishnah.
Vilna variants: 6:4.21 reads ואם; 6:4.23 reads עושה; Vilna lacks the citation label (תהלים קכח).

Vilna adds at the end of this mishnah the sayings the base numbers 6:5: אל תבקש גדולה לעצמך ואל תחמוד כבוד יותר מלמודך עשה ואל תתאוה לשלחנם של מלכים ששולחנך גדול משולחנם וכתרך גדול מכתרם ונאמן הוא בעל מלאכתך שישלם לך שכר פעולתך.

phrases.english: Do not seek greatness for yourself
Do not crave the table of kings
for your table is greater than their table
and your crown is greater than their crown
and the master of your work is faithful
to pay you the reward of your labor

grammar: אַל + imperfect (תְּבַקֵּשׁ, תַּחְמֹד, תִּתְאַוֶּה) is the negative command, "do not ..."; the one positive command is the bare imperative עֲשֵׂה.
יוֹתֵר מִלִּמּוּדְךָ עֲשֵׂה has the comparative phrase before the verb: "more than your learning, do".
לְשֻׁלְחָנָם שֶׁל מְלָכִים has a pleonastic suffix ("their table, of kings") with the genitive particle שֶׁל, as in 6:2 and 6:4.
The two comparisons שֶׁשֻּׁלְחָנְךָ גָדוֹל מִשֻּׁלְחָנָם and וְכִתְרְךָ גָדוֹל מִכִּתְרָם use מִן with an adjective for "greater than"; the "table" and "crown" are those of Torah (the scholar's own).
segments.note: יוֹתֵר מִלִּמּוּדְךָ עֲשֵׂה is ambiguous: "act more than you study" (let practice exceed learning), or "do more than your learning requires". The English "do more than you learn" keeps the compression. בַּעַל מְלַאכְתְּךָ is "the master (employer) of your work"; by context it is God, and the English leaves it literal. שֶׁיְּשַׁלֵּם after נֶאֱמָן is "faithful ... to pay".
apparatus: Vilna's text differs in arrangement. The sayings of the base 6:5 (אַל תְּבַקֵּשׁ ... שְׂכַר פְּעֻלָּתֶךָ) stand in Vilna at the end of 6:4 (see the apparatus there).

In their place Vilna's 6:5 reads גדולה תורה יותר מן הכהונה ומן המלכות ..., the opening of the base 6:6 with the list of the forty-eight things. Its גדולה is therefore the adjective 'great' (גְּדוֹלָה תוֹרָה, 'Torah is greater'), not the noun גְּדֻלָּה 'greatness' that the alignment pairs it with at 6:5.3; at 6:5.4-7 it reads תורה, and from 6:5.9 on מן הכהונה ומן המלכות שהמלכות נקנית ...

segments.english: Torah is greater than the priesthood and than kingship, for kingship is acquired by thirty degrees, and the priesthood by twenty-four, but the Torah is acquired by forty-eight things. And these are they: by study, by hearing with the ear, by ordering the lips, by understanding of the heart, by discernment of the heart, by awe, by reverence, by humility, by joy, by purity, by serving the sages, by exact discussion with colleagues, and by the sharp debate of the students; by composure, by Scripture, by Mishnah; by little business, by little worldly occupation, by little pleasure, by little sleep, by little talk, by little laughter; by patience, by a good heart, by faith in the sages, and by accepting sufferings. One who knows his place, and who is glad in his portion, and who makes a fence around his words, and does not claim credit for himself; beloved, a lover of the Omnipresent, a lover of creatures, a lover of acts of righteousness, a lover of upright dealings, a lover of reproofs; who keeps far from honor, and does not puff up his heart over his learning, and does not take pleasure in giving rulings; who bears the yoke with his fellow, tips him toward the scale of merit, sets him on the truth, and sets him on peace; whose heart is settled in his study; who asks and answers, hears and adds; who learns in order to teach and who learns in order to practice; who makes his teacher wiser, and who sets what he has heard exactly right, and who says a thing in the name of the one who said it. Thus you have learned that whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption to the world, as it is said (Esther 2): "And Esther said to the king in the name of Mordecai."

grammar: נִקְנֵית is a Nifal passive participle, "is acquired (bought)"; the three acquisitions, kingship, priesthood and Torah, are measured by a number of מַעֲלוֹת "degrees" (kingship 30, priesthood 24, with מַעֲלוֹת understood in the second clause) and דְבָרִים "things" (Torah 48).

The long list is a series of nouns, each with the preposition בְּ- "by, with, in", then a run of participles (הַמַּכִּיר, הַשָּׂמֵחַ, הָעוֹשֶׂה ...), with the article, describing the person who acquires Torah; the participles are in the nominative absolute with no verb, listing qualities rather than steps.

בְּמִעוּט ("with little of ...") repeats six times; בְּ- with an abstract noun gives the means or manner. The pairs that name states of mind (אֵימָה, יִרְאָה, עֲנָוָה, שִׂמְחָה, טָהֳרָה) are plain abstract nouns with בְּ-.
מִתְרַחֵק, מִתְיַשֵּׁב are Hitpael participles (reflexive: "distances himself", "settles"); לִבּוֹ is the subject of מִתְיַשֵּׁב and the object of מֵגִיס ("makes his heart proud, puffs up").
הָא לָמַדְתָּ ("so you have learned") closes the series by drawing a conclusion; שֶׁכָּל הָאוֹמֵר ... מֵבִיא is a general principle proved by Esther 2:22.
segments.note: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ in בְּמִעוּט דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ is "worldly occupation" (lit. "the way of the land"), as the decisions require, a general term for earning a living and social intercourse; the English keeps it as "worldly occupation". אָהוּב and the participles that follow belong to the same list of descriptions without a conjunction; the English joins them with semicolons. הַמְכַוֵּן אֶת שְׁמוּעָתוֹ is ambiguous: "directs/aligns what he has heard" (gets it exactly right) or "directs his hearing to the point"; the English chooses the first. מַכְרִיעוֹ לְכַף זְכוּת is the idiom of judging someone favorably: the scales are tipped to the side of merit. הַצְּדָקוֹת, plural, may be "acts of charity"; the English chooses "acts of righteousness". סְיָג is a fence, a protective restriction.
apparatus: Esther 2:22, quoted from the Hebrew of the mishnah.

Vilna variants: 6:6.72 סייג; 6:6.90 and 6:6.93 are swapped in order (Vilna reads התוכחות where the base has הַמֵּישָׁרִים, and conversely); 6:6.105 בעול; 6:6.107 חבירו; 6:6.114 מעמידו (without ו); 6:6.135 והמכוין; 6:6.150 גאולה.

Vilna places 6:6.1-65 in the preceding mishnah (its 6:5, after the opening גדולה תורה). Its text there also lacks וְאֵלוּ הֵן and בְּטָהֳרָה, omits סְחוֹרָה, and reads the items שינה, שיחה, תענוג, שחוק, דרך ארץ in that order (the base reads סְחוֹרָה, דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, תַּעֲנוּג, שֵׁינָה, שִׂיחָה, שְׂחוֹק).
